paragraphs: Caution signals | This page corresponds to O*NET-SOC 37-2011.00, Janitors and Cleaners, Except Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners. The official scope is to keep buildings clean and orderly; perform heavy cleaning such as cleaning floors, shampooing carpets, washing walls and glass, and removing refuse; duties may include tending furnaces and boilers, performing routine maintenance, notifying management of repair needs, and clearing snow or debris from sidewalks. The occupation is marked Bright Outlook. Core deliverables are cleaning and maintenance results meeting standards and safety requirements, rather than merely looking clean. Risks arise from chemical preparation and use, powered equipment and electricity, slippery surfaces and work at height, and hygiene and infection control in restrooms and refuse areas. Under this page's evidence policy, U.S. wages are not fixed as static figures; consult the current O*NET 37-2011.00 national wage page. U.S. employment and outlook show approximately 2,447,700 employed in 2024, below-average growth for 2024—2034 (1%—2%), and 351,300 projected openings. Exact occupational wages for mainland China were not obtained (recorded here as a visible data gap) and are recorded as a visible evidence gap. If physical demands, shift work, and chemical exposure are difficult for you to tolerate, treat them as practical costs requiring serious consideration.

Taking responsibility for judgments | Fit depends on whether you can do three things within the same assignment: perform sound cleaning and maintenance (sweep, mop, strip wax and polish, shampoo carpets, dust, and remove refuse by area and standard, treat stains, document anomalies and repair needs, and produce reviewable work records); manage safety and standards (follow standards and organizational policies for chemical preparation and labeling, equipment and electrical safety, slip prevention and warnings, protective equipment, work at height and outdoors, and compliance boundaries for pest control and fumigation); and accept clearly defined job responsibilities (take responsibility for your work quality and safety, and seek guidance or refer equipment repairs, pest treatment, or system changes beyond your authority). Test this through a verifiable exercise, such as preparing a cleaning work and safety checklist for an entirely fictional floor and stain scenario, rather than relying only on an interest questionnaire.

To assess whether this occupation suits you, first conduct a verifiable exercise using public or simulated materials: create an entirely fictional floor and cleaning needs, and outline the process from confirming areas and standards, checking chemical and equipment safety, sweeping and polishing according to procedures, and handling stains and anomalies to requesting supplies and handing over. Mark checks and possible problems at each step (incorrect chemical concentrations or labels, equipment and wiring hazards, no wet-floor warnings, inadequate work-at-height and exterior-wall protection, and unauthorized repairs or pesticide use). Afterwards, check whether chemical and equipment safety, warnings and protection, anomaly reporting, and authorization boundaries are indispensable; repairs or pest treatment beyond your authority are referred or submitted for guidance; and the process leaves reviewable records. All materials must be fictional; do not perform actual work at height or mix chemicals.

Fit signals | Work activities in O*NET 37-2011.00 primarily involve communicating with supervisors and colleagues, organizing and prioritizing, general physical activity, inspecting equipment and materials, and processing information. If you are willing to consistently perform physical cleaning and maintenance to standards, attend to detail and safety, and understand and follow chemical and equipment instructions, these daily requirements may align with your working style. Interest and personality tools are only for designing trials; they cannot determine hiring eligibility or performance.

Janitors and building cleaners, excluding maids and housekeeping cleaners, correspond to O*NET-SOC 37-2011.00, Janitors and Cleaners, Except Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners. The official scope is to keep buildings clean and orderly; perform heavy cleaning such as cleaning floors, shampooing carpets, washing walls and glass, and removing refuse; duties may include tending furnaces and boilers, performing routine maintenance, notifying management of repair needs, and clearing snow or debris from sidewalks. A typical complete workflow is to confirm areas and standards, check chemical and equipment safety, sweep and polish, handle stains and anomalies, and request supplies and hand over. Current U.S. national pay: a 2025 median of $36,840 per year; employment of 2,432,600 in 2025, 2% growth for 2025—2035, and 321,800 average annual openings (an overall projection, not attributed to AI). The exact occupational wage gap for China remains; industry averages are broad references only.

entries: Objects of work | Clean and perform routine maintenance within safety and quality standards, working with floors and walls, carpets and furniture, restrooms and refuse, cleaning chemicals and powered equipment, and building safety inspection items.

Checkable outputs | Cleaning and maintenance results that meet standards, chemical and equipment use records, supply and consumable requests, anomaly and repair-need reports, and handover and inspection records. Results must be traceable to area standards and working conditions.
Complete workflow | Confirm areas and standards → check chemical and equipment safety → sweep and polish → handle stains and anomalies → request supplies and hand over.

paragraphs: Key judgments | O*NET work context data show: wearing common protective or safety equipment daily, 84%; walking or running continually or almost continually, 61%; face-to-face discussions daily, 57%; handling objects and tools continually or almost continually, 56%; very high responsibility for others' health and safety, 47%; and exactness or accuracy very important, 50%. Judgments rely on area cleaning standards, chemical and equipment instructions, and protection and operational safety requirements.

Environment and pace | Work primarily involves on-site physical activity: indoors in a controlled environment daily, 79%; standing continually or almost continually, 47%; exposure to disease or infections daily, 43%; repetitive motions more than half the time, 42%; substantial freedom to schedule tasks, 58%; substantial freedom to make decisions, 51%; and coordinating or leading others not important at all, 29%. Shifts and facility use schedules drive the pace.

Research inputs | O*NET 37-2011.00 provides the precise occupational identity, tasks, work activities, and work context. The interest code is RC (Realistic—Conventional), and the occupation is in Job Zone Three (the page lists education requirements qualitatively, without exact percentages) and is marked Bright Outlook. The main industries are administrative and support services and educational services. Current U.S. national pay: a 2025 median of $36,840 per year; employment of 2,432,600 in 2025, 2% growth for 2025—2035, and 321,800 average annual openings (an overall projection, not attributed to AI). The exact occupational wage gap for China remains; industry averages are broad references only.

The first checks concern the objects (floors and walls, restrooms and refuse, chemicals and equipment), inputs (area cleaning standards, chemical and equipment instructions, and protection and safety requirements), and deliverables (cleaning results that meet standards, equipment and consumable records, and anomaly reporting and handover records). Anything unverified must remain pending verification; intuition based on experience cannot replace chemical instructions and safety requirements.

Assess the complete workflow in four steps: check inputs (confirm area standards, chemical and equipment condition, and safety conditions) → define the task (work only within authorization, without unauthorized repair or treatment) → execute and document (clean to standard with an audit trail) → review and escalate (stop immediately and report chemical or equipment anomalies, damaged facilities, or safety hazards). A complete workflow requires verifiable standards, instructions, and authorization, rather than merely a clean-looking surface.

Boundaries with neighboring roles | This page covers only the precise occupation O*NET-SOC 37-2011.00, Janitors and Cleaners, Except Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners. Neighboring occupations such as dishwashers, first-line supervisors of housekeeping and janitorial workers, maids and housekeeping cleaners, landscaping and groundskeeping workers, and carpet installers differ in their objects of work, authorized scope, and responsibilities. They cannot be interchanged based solely on titles, and proxy categories cannot replace organizational authorization, qualifications, or ultimate responsibility.

Positive signals | You can follow procedures to sweep, polish, shampoo carpets, dust, and remove refuse; check chemical and equipment conditions and identify stains and safety hazards; and preserve reviewable anomaly and repair-need records and hand work over accurately.

Caution conditions | Risk signals include mixing chemicals based on experience, neglecting equipment and electrical safety, inadequate wet-floor and work-at-height protection, failing to report damaged facilities and safety hazards, and unauthorized repairs or pesticide use. Conclusion | Activity preferences align more closely with a combination of hands-on work and following procedures (O*NET interest code RC). However, interest codes can only help design trials; they cannot determine hiring eligibility or performance.

Conclusion | This page provides no validation evidence that personality tests predict performance in this occupation. Continue checking against real tasks, responsibility boundaries, and reviewable deliverables rather than drawing conclusions from a single label.

Conclusion | RIASEC or personality frameworks can only help formulate questions; they cannot replace work samples, learning ability, qualifications, and actual performance evidence for this occupation. No tool conclusion constitutes a hiring, authorization, or appointment decision.

Chemical risk | Do not mix different cleaning chemicals; check labels, SDS, training, and specified protection before use. Prepare solutions only according to product dilution instructions. Stop using and report unknown bottles, missing labels, or uncertainty first. OSHA / NIOSH recommendations are U.S. safety references, not Chinese statutory permission: https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA3512.pdf.

Equipment and electrical risk | Trigger: improper use or lack of inspection of powered cleaning equipment, boilers, and electrical equipment. Consequences: possible electric shock, mechanical injuries, or fire. Controls: inspect equipment and wiring before use, follow operating instructions, and stop using and report anomalies immediately. Boundary: qualified personnel must handle equipment repairs and system adjustments.

Slippery surfaces and height risk | Set up wet-floor warnings; ladder or height tasks require checks of specific training, equipment, site protection, and authorization. Stop and report when these cannot be confirmed; having someone watch is not sufficient protection.

Hygiene exposure risk | Follow area infection control requirements and training for protection, cleaning, and disinfection. Medical waste, sharps, and unknown items must not be treated as ordinary refuse; refer them to authorized personnel. Frequency of disease exposure is not an infection rate.

Common escalation rule | Whenever chemical, equipment, or safety conditions are insufficient, first stop the relevant step and hand over the facts, impacts, and unresolved issues in reviewable records to an authorized responsible person. Do not override safety requirements, professional opinions, or organizational authorization, or substitute model output for on-site safety judgments.

career_risk_cards.heading: Work risks and boundaries for janitors and building cleaners, excluding maids and housekeeping cleaners

risks.affected_roles: Janitors and Building Cleaners, Except Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners
risks.consequence: May cause skin or respiratory injuries or dangerous reactions.
risks.mitigation: Do not mix different cleaning chemicals; first check labels, SDS, and training. Stop using and report unknown or unlabeled products.
risks.scenario: Mixing cleaning agents based on experience, incorrect concentrations or labels, or inadequate ventilation.

risks.affected_roles: Janitors and Building Cleaners, Except Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners
risks.consequence: May cause electric shock, mechanical injuries, or fire.
risks.mitigation: Inspect equipment and wiring before use, follow operating instructions, and stop using and report anomalies immediately.
risks.scenario: Improper use or lack of inspection of powered cleaning equipment, boilers, and electrical equipment.

risks.affected_roles: Janitors and Building Cleaners, Except Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners
risks.consequence: May cause slip or fall injuries.
risks.mitigation: Set up wet-floor warnings; check training, equipment, protection, and authorization before ladder or height tasks, and stop if conditions are insufficient.
risks.scenario: No wet-floor warning, or inadequate protection for step-stool or work-at-height tasks.

risks.affected_roles: Janitors and Building Cleaners, Except Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners
risks.consequence: May cause exposure to disease or infection.
risks.mitigation: Check area infection control and protection; refer medical waste, sharps, and unknown items to authorized personnel.
risks.scenario: Inadequate protection when cleaning restrooms, medical areas, or refuse areas.

risks.affected_roles: Janitors and Building Cleaners, Except Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners
risks.mitigation: Complete inspections and audit trails through the required process; rushing does not replace safety.
risks.scenario: Skipping building safety inspections under shift and site schedule pressure.

risks.affected_roles: Janitors and Building Cleaners, Except Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners
risks.consequence: May override safety requirements, professional opinions, or organizational authorization.
risks.mitigation: First stop the relevant step and hand over facts, impacts, and unresolved issues to an authorized responsible person.
risks.scenario: Continuing despite insufficient chemical, equipment, or safety conditions.

title.text: Evaluating Janitorial and Building Cleaning, Except Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners, as a Career: Work, Entry, and Risk Boundaries

subject.name: Janitors and Building Cleaners, Except Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners
subject.summary: Janitors and building cleaners, excluding maids and housekeeping cleaners, keep buildings clean and orderly; perform heavy cleaning such as cleaning floors, shampooing carpets, washing walls and glass, and removing refuse; and may tend furnaces and boilers, perform routine maintenance, notify management of repair needs, and clear snow or debris from sidewalks. Work includes confirming areas and standards, checking chemical and equipment safety, sweeping and polishing, handling stains and anomalies, and requesting supplies and handing over. Under this page's evidence policy, U.S. wages are not fixed as static figures; a current O*NET 37-2011.00 query entry point is provided. U.S. employment and outlook show approximately 2,447,700 employed in 2024, below-average growth for 2024—2034 at 1%—2%, and 351,300 projected openings; the occupation is marked Bright Outlook. Exact occupational wages for mainland China were not obtained (recorded here as a visible data gap) and are recorded as a visible evidence gap.
